doc.title: Benny Golson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Working with Bernard Purdie, Richard Tee and Eric Gale on rock and R&B sessions
summary: Golson wrote for top pop-session players, who interpreted his music; he recalls Purdie's 'Pretty Purdie, the Hitmaker' sign.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: What caught my eye is the drummer. You see Bernard Purdie playing some of these – then you’ve got Richard Tee.
I did a lot with them. Not just this here. That realm of rock-and-roll, rhythm­ and-blues. We did a lot of things, Bernard Purdie and Richard Tee. What was the guitar player?
Eric Gale. We did a lot of stuff that people wouldn’t associate with Benny Golson. Here, let me give this to you.
Let me put it back over here.
We did a lot of stuff like that.
What was it like working with those guys? That’s not really in the genre or style that’s most associated with you.

They were good at it. So the level was so good – excellence is excellence, no matter where you find it. So it was great working with them. I never recorded playing with them, because that wasn’t really my cup of tea. I didn’t know how to do that too well. But I wrote the stuff, they interpreted it, and it always worked out great. That Bernard Purdie, he could do anything. He used to have his stand that he would bring. He had a sign made. Whenever he played, he’d set the stand up and put the sign on it. The sign said, “Pretty Purdie, the Hitmaker.” On every session, he’d set the stand up and put the sign on it.
So they could see it. Sure. “Pretty Purdie, the Hitmaker.” You get the alliteration there?
“Pretty Purdie.” But he could – oh, he lived up to it. That guy – he had that stuff down.
With Eric Gale and Richard Tee – those guys. Yes indeed.
